text: Nearly every practical QML system described in this course is, structurally, a classical program with a quantum circuit called as a subroutine. This lesson names that structure explicitly and traces exactly where control passes between classical and quantum code during training.

One hybrid training iteration, step by step. Classically, load a batch of data and encode it. Then the quantum device runs the circuit at the current parameters, returning an expectation value. Classically again, compute the loss. Then the quantum device runs the circuit again at each shifted parameter to get the parameter-shift gradient terms, and classically, assemble the full gradient and run one optimizer step. Every quantum step hands back one number; every classical step hands back new parameters.

It would be convenient if the whole loop ran entirely on quantum hardware, but that isn't possible today: nothing about the parameter-shift rule or standard optimizers like Adam has a known way to run as a quantum circuit — gradient aggregation and optimizer state updates are ordinary classical arithmetic. This is why calling QML hybrid, rather than fully quantum, is accurate, not a hedge: there is currently no end-to-end quantum ML training loop with zero classical computation in it.

Every round-trip between the classical host and the quantum device costs real time. A circuit with k parameters needs 2k quantum-side evaluations per gradient step, plus whatever classical-side computation assembles them. On real cloud-accessed hardware, each round trip can also mean queueing time behind other users' jobs — a cost a purely classical model training on local or cloud GPUs simply doesn't have.
Next lesson gets concrete about how this loop is actually implemented: treating a quantum circuit as one differentiable layer inside an otherwise ordinary PyTorch or TensorFlow model.
